In this study, we investigate the two-layer neural network approach for calculating the lowest eigenvalue and corresponding eigenfunction of the one-dimensional Schrödinger equation. We find that initial node positioning significantly influences the overall model performance. We also investigate how the eigenvalue loss landscape's non-convex nature affects outcome generalization. Our analysis demonstrates that eigenfunctions with nodal lines exhibit distinct symmetry-related properties.

The authors are considering a thin-layer homogenization problem in two or more dimensions. This problem involves solving the Laplace equation for a domain formed by taking one large domain and adding numerous layers of alternating high and low contrast material with very low thickness. All other properties of these inclusion materials assume high contrast and their internal geometries replicate those of reference shapes within those materials. These shapes can be either homogeneous throughout or heterogeneous and composed of multiple phases. 

When these shapes are the same in every other inclusion, past studies have demonstrated that the macroscopic behavior of such a material can be modeled using effective parameters that incorporate geometrical details from both internal structures and material properties. However, when these shapes are different across inclusions, it has been shown that a simplified two-parameter model is insufficient to describe the system. Instead, an infinite series of parameters is required to achieve satisfactory results. 

In this study, a modification to existing problem settings involves adding layers containing various geometrical and material types around a base domain. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that, in this scenario, adding a large number of such inclusions with geometrical and material types that are not easily divisible by each other can still result in effective parameters that are comparable to those of a single-type inclusion system. This means that a simplified two-parameter model can be used to accurately describe the system, in contrast to cases requiring an infinite series of parameters.

A sophisticated quantum field theory model, known as the Bogoliubov-type Dirac field, is an effective method for describing certain observed phenomena in the universe. We employ this model to study the behavior of the theory within a specific FLRW spacetime scenario. Our analysis reveals the probability of a process where one particle splits into two, and we calculate a corresponding quantum measure called the quantum cosmological wave function. By applying an established approximation, we derive an analytical solution for the wave function's amplitude. Further examination of the derived equations allows us to evaluate the probability of this particle division process. Our results indicate that the division is more likely to occur during a particular FLRW spacetime phase called the matter-dominated phase. We also examine how the theoretical results are influenced by changes in theory parameters.

In pathology, estimating the count of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes is crucial but time-consuming, leading to significant variability in assessments by pathologists. A proposed solution involves using a deep learning method for categorizing tissue images, which can be trained through a federated approach across multiple healthcare institutions. By adapting existing techniques and addressing challenges such as non-identically distributed data and varying image resolutions, the study demonstrates the effectiveness of collaborative model updates without the need for central data sharing. Results indicate a consistent improvement in performance with more participating centers, particularly when using more robust network architectures.

Our investigation focuses on a technique that allows for the rapid creation of intricate magnonic states by combining two techniques: dressing and stretching. We utilize this technique in conjunction with an additional control field to modify the dynamics of the system within a closed system, resulting in the generation of magnonic quantum states analogous to Yuen states and squeezened coherent states. By carefully selecting the parameters of the control field, our protocol enables the generation of magnonic quantum states characterized by reduced noise in specific field components, in addition to non-classical correlations. We demonstrate the application of this state-fabrication technique for tasks such as low-noise magnonic communication and low-magnetic-field atomic magnetometry.

This paper presents a novel framework utilizing Evolutionary Pathway Creation (EPC) to enhance movement capabilities of agents through reinforcement learning, without the need for task-specific adjustments. By embedding a universal policy network capable of adapting to various environments, our method circumvents traditional catastrophic forgetting issues. Each time an agent encounters a new environment, its policy evolves into a unique, environment-specific version, effectively turning every agent into a versatile explorer. Our approach's efficacy is demonstrated by a successful implementation of a quadrupedal robot that can navigate and adapt to diverse scenarios with remarkable efficiency.

Our high-resolution X-ray spectroscopic data from the XMM-Newton Observatory, obtained at a low brightness mode, reveal a significant thermal component at a high-temperature of 1.6 keV within the central region of NGC 7213's 1.5 kpc jet.  This hot gas is concentrated in a high-density area with a density of 10^-3 cm^-3, characterized by a high aspect ratio of 1.5, strongly suggesting that it is a result of interaction between the jet and the surrounding ambient medium.  Using the maximum entropy method, we determined that the hot gas is moving at a speed of 200 km/s, consistent with simulations of radiative shocks in low-entropy jets, which implies a dense and cool environment surrounding the hot gas.  This is the first direct observation of a warm phase in a relativistic jet, offering valuable insights into the complex interplay between jets and their surrounding medium.

This research introduces a two-phase method for the model-independent reconfiguration of a nonlinear optimal controller. Initially, a model-free approach is employed to identify the optimal state variables and their corresponding tangent linear model, which is then utilized in the second phase to find the optimal tangent linear model and reconstruct the original nonlinear optimal controller. The novel two-phase method is compared to a existing single-phase strategy, in which the model-free learning of optimal state variables is maintained, but fails to recover the original nonlinear optimal controller. The outcome of this comparison demonstrates that the two-phase method is capable of not only detecting system faults but also restoring a optimally operated system to its former performance.

The SiD sensor, a powerful detector concept for the 100 TeV future hadron collider, has distinct features: its massive central solenoid magnet and forward detectors placed in heavy magnetic fields. To enhance the siD's performance and adapt it to various physics scenarios, an investigation was conducted to optimize the sensor's overall design. Key areas of focus included the solenoid magnet's strength, its structural support system, and innovations in support materials and endcaps, as well as innovations in the detector's central plane support material.

We analyzed the stars in Tonantzintla 2, a globular cluster in the Milky Way, to understand its metal content and the rate at which it rotates. We used high-quality spectra of 42 of its member stars, and found that most have low or slightly higher metal content and are fast rotators. The data shows that T2 has lower metal content and is less concentrated than similar groups. T2 has 11 rapidly spinning members with the highest rate of rotation reaching 160 km/s. The distribution of metals and rotation within T2 does not show a connection. Our results suggest that T2 has a more relaxed structure and is not as dense as groups with similar metal content. T2 is similar to other groups with two distinct populations, and we suggest it has a similar age and metal content, but more research is needed to confirm this. T2 is located in a region with many other groups and we used our data to understand their properties. T2 is located in a group with many other groups and we used our data to understand their properties.

Earth observation has been revolutionized by the introduction of open data from high-resolution satellite imagery, terrestrial sensors, and the cloud storage infrastructure, which together have facilitated the application of deep learning. However, the promise of deep learning has yet to be fully realized in Earth monitoring due to several limitations, including fragmented computing resources, inefficient data processing, and limited access to visualization tools. To address these challenges, this paper proposes EarthNets, a system designed to simplify and accelerate Earth monitoring through the virtualization of distributed computing resources. EarthNets enables users to create and manage multiple isolated networks for training, testing, and deploying deep learning models. These networks can be accessed through a web interface and are supported by a container-based architecture. The proposed system is evaluated through the integration of a live demo, which is further detailed in this paper.

We establish a systematic framework for formulating renormalization group equations applicable to active nematics in three dimensions in the vicinity of criticality. These equations account for all relevant factors, particularly those driving the anisotropy of viscosity and diffusion. Our analysis reveals that while four-point processes contribute to anomalous transport, they do so at a level insignificant compared to the anisotropy's influence. Consequently, our framework effectively encompasses and explains previously observed phenomena.

Identifying abnormal readings in time series data is crucial in numerous industries. Existing methods, however, are often limited by their reliance on time-consuming dynamic time warping or ineffective unsupervised techniques. To address these issues, we present a novel supervised method called ReAD that efficiently detects local anomalies in time series. This approach divides time series data into adaptable sub-sections and evaluates them to pinpoint irregularities. Our algorithm's performance is thoroughly examined on open-source datasets, including Drosophila, ECG2STL, and SMAC, with comparative results against eight other methods. Drosophila data in particular highlights the significant advantages of our approach. Additionally, we provide a detailed analysis of the effects of hyperparameter choices on performance.

The impact of the pion vector form factor on the low-energy hadronic interaction, particularly considering the final state interaction between the two pions, is investigated. A new parameterization of the pion vector form factor is developed based on threshold behavior and is compared with other common approaches. This form factor is incorporated into calculations of the hadronic vacuum polarization contribution to the muon's anomalous magnetic moment. The difference between the two approaches is significant at high energies but negligible at relevant energies for $(g-2)$ calculations. The difference amounts to less than 0.2% in the integral of the vacuum polarization.

We introduce Universal embodiment for Code (UCO), a theory that views programs as having a tangible form in the environments they operate in. According to UCO, long-term program execution can be likened to navigation and interaction within a complex, multi-step process. UCO's principles enable researchers to identify and categorize various skills a program acquires during its execution, ultimately allowing for a test of whether these skills can be transferred to new tasks. Our study reveals that code running in web interfaces develops 'virtual' user interfaces tailored to their respective applications, and these interfaces contain transferable skills that enable code to perform tasks like navigating web pages, clicking buttons, and inputting data. Our findings demonstrate the capability of code to transfer learned skills in actual programming tasks and provide a testing ground for future research in program embodiment.

We investigated the relationship between galaxy shapes and their mass, 
as well as the mass of their surrounding galaxy halos, using large, high-quality datasets.
Two key factors were considered: the ratio of light in a galaxy's outer areas compared to its center,
and the mass of its host halo.
This study utilized comprehensive, high-quality datasets from two major galaxy surveys,
resulting in a substantial dataset of 1070 galaxies.
Our in-depth analysis revealed that galaxies with more extended light distributions,
tend to reside in more massive halos,
especially within certain ranges of satellite count.
Furthermore, a similar trend was observed when accounting for galaxy color,
with both red and blue galaxy samples displaying the same halo mass dependence on shape,
light distribution, and number of satellites,
regardless of their initial color.
These findings imply that physical processes, rather than just a single factor,
are responsible for the observed trends.

A significant challenge in climate science is accurately quantifying the cooling effect that aerosols have on Earth. Researchers have been exploring innovative methods to measure this impact, such as using high-frequency star brightness data to assess how aerosols scatter light. To establish a foundation for this research, we developed an automated system that monitors star frequencies and calculates light scattering from both intentional and natural changes in aerosol distribution. Our results indicate that a database of 77 stars yielded reliable estimates of light scattering, with a mean absolute error of 1.5% and variability of ±1.5%. To further validate these findings, we used simulated changes in cloud distribution based on a specific fire event that occurred in 2019. Our analysis showed that using backscatter values derived from stellar observations resulted in a 10% underestimation of aerosol measurements obtained from a lidar instrument, with comparable results when comparing radiometric data. Our approach has the potential to fill a data gap where traditional instruments cannot provide adequate coverage, such as in areas with challenging access or during extreme weather conditions.

The GGLasso Python library provides a comprehensive solution for feature selection and correlation analysis, addressing the limitations of traditional graphical models in dealing with complex data, including missing values and diverse data types. Based on the generalized graphical lasso algorithm, the framework enables the simultaneous analysis of multiple datasets or mixed-type datasets. The framework within GGLasso includes functions for data preprocessing, model training, and inference, complemented by utility tools for dataset evaluation, such as predictive performance assessment, posterior distribution estimation, and precision-recall curves generation. With these capabilities, the framework optimizes graphical model utility, as demonstrated through several practical applications showcasing its effectiveness in real-world scenarios.

To understand the origin of planetary masses, two competing theories are under investigation: planetesimal formation triggered by gravitational instability (GI) and gradual accretion from a disk. By analyzing the photoevaporation and magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) models of the TW Hydrae system, we can determine which mechanism is responsible for the observed emission. Specifically, photoevaporation produces a narrow, hot component that originates close to the star, whereas MHD disks generate broader structures due to their larger radii. Although both mechanisms share similarities, such as temperature and molecular content, distinguishing between them is crucial. With advancements in high-angular resolution radio astronomy, such as the combination of ALMA and the VLA, we can achieve the necessary resolution to distinguish these features and gain insight into the formation of planetary masses.

A novel method combining data-driven and model-based techniques is proposed to
identify speech segments and track fundamental frequency without supervision.
Key components of this approach involve the development of dynamic systems,
statistical testers and estimators, which are applied to feature-extracted speech
data. Specifically, initial segments are determined by analyzing whether the
data conform to a noise model or a harmonic model. The speech segmentation
sequence is then established using the Viterbi algorithm based on these models.
The system also utilizes a Kalman filter to estimate fundamental frequency. The
effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated with experimental results.

We introduce a new, accelerated forward-reverse algorithm to solve a broad category of monotone inclusion problems. By blending the advantages of the inertial forward-reverse and the proximal reverse operators, our algorithm capitalizes on the initial gap sequence from the former to expedite convergence and employs the more efficient Yosida approximation for the bifunction. This results in improved numerical performance and reduced computational costs. To ensure stability and rapid convergence rates, we derive specific step-size conditions using a dynamical weighting approach. This strategy allows for the derivation of step-size restrictions solely based on initial problem parameters, eliminating the need for ad-hoc parameter adjustments.

A new calculation of two-loop Higgs masses in a specific type of theoretical model, the NR-MSSM, is presented in this work. The model, in turn, is based on an even simpler framework, the NMSSM, which itself addresses a fundamental problem in the Standard Model by explaining the origin of fermion masses, particularly those of neutrinos. What sets this new model apart is that it incorporates additional matter superfields in pairs, thereby enabling the generation of a non-zero neutrino mass without violating lepton number conservation. The presented calculation builds upon the work of a previous study by R. Kitano and R. Sato, expanding its scope to include additional relevant terms in the theoretical model's superpotential.

Recent advancements in research have led to a surge in employing neural networks for a wide range of tasks, and automatically creating such models has also gained attention. The development of neural networks, like other complex systems, benefits from innovations in Generative Design Search (GDS), which explores the effect of architectural changes on task performance. This process involves not only optimizing existing architectures but also considering novel designs, and our research focuses on integrating Principles of Attribute Directed Synthesis (ADS) into this process. By integrating ADS principles, we can automate much of the design process, and our proposed method, AdaNeuSyn, uses this framework to efficiently discover high-performance neural architectures, and our experiments demonstrate its effectiveness and robustness in producing better results than state-of-the-art GDS methods.

In the future of wireless communication, millimeter wave (mmWave) networks are expected to play a crucial role. To efficiently utilize these networks, a single base station will use a multi-panel setup with multiple radio frequency chains to support a large number of mobile terminals. Designing effective broadcasting schemes to optimize system performance is a key challenge. This paper investigates broadcasting protocols for a scenario where the same content needs to be delivered to several groups of users. The authors compare two hybrid broadcasting protocols, one with separate beams for each group and another with a single beam serving all groups. The analysis of the second protocol shows that it achieves near-optimal performance at a lower data rate. This significant performance gain highlights the value of a unified approach to broadcasting in mmWave networks.

Deep learning models extracted from centralized training can be太大 for devices with limited resources, leading to inefficient communication in distributed inference tasks. Researchers have attempted to address this issue by creating smaller models, but their efforts have been hindered by significant performance drops. This drop in performance necessitates more data labeling and increased communication between servers and client devices, ultimately resulting in a counterproductive outcome. This paper introduces a new approach to mitigate these challenges, focusing on developing a method for creating smaller models that retain the predictive capabilities of their larger counterparts. This method, known as Federated Extraction, leverages the power of Federated Learning to train a smaller model in collaboration with multiple larger models, each implanted on different devices, without revealing any sensitive data, thereby producing a compact and effective model suitable for inference tasks, as demonstrated by a case study on model compression for the ResNet-50 architecture, with results indicating improved performance and communication efficiency.

In Next Generation Networks, the Named Data Architecture (NDN) is a key component, and its performance can be significantly enhanced by integrating it with Computing in Network Edge (COMNET) at the edge network. Our research focuses on coordinating an unbounded number of NDN routers and edge computing servers dynamically in a network with uncertain incoming traffic. We developed an adaptive control strategy that balances the loads across NDN routers and COMNET servers by regulating forwarding policies and activating/commissioning server resources. Our findings show that the proposed approach ensures near-optimal, stable operation of the network, and its efficiency is verified through simulations.

This research investigates the Cauchy problem for an elastic, mass-spring system on a tree-like structure. The model under consideration involves an elastic beam, linked at a central point with edges of finite length and damped by infinite masses. We demonstrate the well-posedness of the initial value problem, and using energy methods, we establish exponential stability for the system's solutions.

In the quark-meson model with U(1)_A symmetry breaking, we analyze multiple phases including normal, superconducting, and supersuperconducting. We discover a novel homogeneous supersuperconducting phase and investigate how it interacts with other phases in the phase diagram. We then examine the properties of these phases near the normal-superconducting boundary under various conditions, such as increasing baryon density at zero temperature or zero density at zero baryon number. We analyze the quark and meson content of the supersuperconducting phase and its interactions with other phases. We also investigate the phase boundary between the normal and superconducting sectors when the U(1)_A symmetry is explicitly disrupted by a theta angle, and we contrast this disruption with the zero theta angle case.

Recent theoretical research has suggested a new type of topological insulator known as electron-type and anion-supported, and is now referred to as electron frameworks. These are exemplified by compounds MTl4Te3 (M = Cd, Hg). Our findings indicate that this novel class of topological insulators is stable, with CdTe2 and Tl2Te being semiconductors, and CdTe and TlTe being semimetals. Notably, the topological properties of these materials are consistent, with their topological character decreasing in the order of SnSb2Te2 > MTl4Te3 (M = Cd, Hg). Our density functional theory calculations have shown that the topological properties are primarily driven by Tl and Te atoms, with the 6p orbitals of Tl and Te being the primary contributors, and the gap size is influenced by the relative position of these 6p bands.

Machine learning's utility function learning approach enables systems to adapt objectives based on operator preferences without explicit programming. However, operator-defined priorities are often not easily quantifiable and can be hard to communicate. Furthermore, most existing utility function learning methods are not well-suited for engineering contexts where operator knowledge is limited. To address these challenges, this research presents a two-pronged approach. Firstly, it proposes expressing utility functions in terms of 'easy to understand' qualitative parameters. Secondly, it introduces a method to incorporate expert knowledge to constrain exploratory learning through a structured exploration space. Through a case study on gear design, the approach's efficacy is demonstrated, yielding a gear with superior performance characteristics and the ability to learn a valid utility function within a restricted and meaningful parameter space.

Recent breakthroughs in adversarial attacks on classification models have been significant, but similar approaches against more sophisticated systems like reinforcement learning agents are yet to be explored. We bridge this gap by developing two novel attack methods for blackbox reinforcement learning setups. Our first attack strategy utilizes the knowledge of an agent's update process, while our second method relies on an assessment of the environment dynamics. To validate these techniques, we successfully applied them to various reward functions in benchmark problems, using both established and recently developed evaluation protocols. Our experiments demonstrate that our attack methods outperform state-of-the-art blackbox approaches, yielding substantial improvements in multiple testing scenarios.

Our research explores the theoretical Lattice Belief Lattice (BLL) theory in two-dimensional crystalline materials, offering mathematical proof that any given BLL pattern contains specific types of symmetries inherent to its lattice structure. Through BLL analysis, we discovered Dirac points formed by intersecting surface states in certain latches, characterized by non-trivial surface topological indices. By incorporating horizontal and vertical glide symmetries, we found Dirac points can only exist in 10 specific wallpaper groups out of a total of 17 possible patterns. Utilizing a dielectric L-shaped structure, we experimentally verified the dielectric surface state exhibits dielectric anti-reflection properties at Dirac point locations across a broad spectrum, with minimal effect from certain surface disruptions. Additionally, the dielectric L-shaped lattice demonstrates latch resonance, a phenomenon in which two photonic bands collapse into a single point within a specified frequency range. This research provides a framework for understanding BLL-based topological states and may offer new insights into the development of complex metamaterials and multi-physical systems.

In order to develop risk-averse policies for non-stationary Markov decision processes, we modify the concept of distortion risk measures, specifically focusing on the family of law-invariant, monotone convex functionals. We then establish a novel equivalent of a key risk control technique - dynamic resentment identification - which serves as the risk-controlled counterpart to value iteration and forms the foundation of our risk-controlled policy iteration process. Our analysis demonstrates the convergence of this process to a unique fixed point, corresponding to the program's value, and further shows the existence of an optimal policy achieving this value. Additionally, our extension of risk control has significant implications, allowing for the risk-controlled policy iteration process to be applied to any complete lattice and its concept can be used to decompose the program into a dynamic system, separating the influence of the program on its value from the impact of initial states.

Business organizations commonly utilize the Jira system to oversee their development projects.  However, researchers have not extensively studied Jira in comparison to other software development tools like GitHub and Gantt projects.  This study undertakes a comprehensive examination of over 17,000 Jira repositories, revealing key insights into public software development trajectories.  The analysis reveals that the majority of projects initiate with a primary objective, represented as an 'Epic', and subsequent issues are created to accomplish this objective.  Our findings indicate that these objectives are typically achieved within 1-2 years.  The research further identifies characteristics of successful projects, including smaller teams, consistent issue creation, and broader topic diversity.  The dataset is made available on the Public dataset.  https://osf.io/v89zk

Distributed Machine Learning is gaining traction for training large-scale neural networks on multiple machines. This paper explores aggregation functions that bridge linear methods, such as averaging, with linear programming-based approaches. Our research reveals a distinct class of aggregation functions characterized by non-decreasing sub-differentiability. This class ensures convexity and enables sub-gradient optimization for any problem defined on a convex domain. Moreover, we establish that smooth and strictly sub-differentiable functions in this class can be represented as compositions of linear and smooth functions,闭合 in U-shape manner. We propose novel, information-efficient, closed-form aggregators within this class, outperforming both traditional and recently proposed alternatives.

We propose and simulate an integrated system to capture and study a solitary atom using a set of carefully designed, overlapping beams of light. The underlying concept involves creating a confined environment where the atom can be trapped in an optical cavity, alongside a series of carefully constructed zones that facilitate the rapid application of light pulses for capturing and manipulating the atom. Our simulation demonstrates the feasibility of this concept through a detailed analysis of the application of specific light pulses and also examines how variations in experimental conditions may impact results. Additionally, we consider the potential for using similar optical techniques to rapidly measure the internal state of the atom by quickly switching between different wavelengths of light.

Let's consider a monoid of words, a monadic second-order theory, and order
relationships between elements within this structure. The MacNeille fulfillment,
denoted as $\mathcal{N}(\Lambda^*)$, represents the pair consisting of the base
set, $\Lambda$, and a corresponding equivalence relation, referred to as the MacNeille
equivalence. The paper in question aims to establish a syntax-based method for
determining the MacNeille equivalence in relation to any given sequence,
specifically within the interval $[\alpha, \beta]$, and subsequently derive the
MacNeille fulfillment, $\alpha \beta$, in the process.

A whole-program approach deduces the molecular structure of a polymer from its
spectral data by starting with polymers of a known class and gradually
introducing more complex structures until the best match for a target spectrum
is found. To illustrate, this method successfully deduces alkanes and alcohols
up to C10 and aliphatic and aromatic compounds up to C15, demonstrating its
applicability to a wide range of chemical structures.

In times of crisis, such as the COVID-19 outbreak, healthcare workers face immense pressure and require creative problem-solving to adapt to rapidly changing environments. A key aspect of this change involves immediate response, where a response time of less than one minute is considered critical. A response within the minute range, however, falls into the 'immediate' category. During the pandemic, there has been a surge in patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), a condition that causes changes in lung compliance. These changes necessitate real-time adjustments in ventilator settings to ensure optimal patient care. To address this challenge, researchers have developed a novel approach called 'immediate positive pressure ventilation,' where settings can be updated within the 'immediate' time frame. A key component of this approach involves the use of adaptive algorithms to analyze end-tidal CO2 (EtCO2) data and provide real-time ventilator settings. The Transfer Function Controller (TFC) algorithm, for example, uses feedback from EtCO2 to adaptively adjust ventilator settings. The effectiveness of this approach has been demonstrated in a case study involving two patients with varying lung compliance. The use of the TFC algorithm enabled the researchers to update ventilator settings within the 'immediate' time frame, ensuring optimal EtCO2 levels and, ultimately, improved patient outcomes. The success of this approach highlights the importance of innovation and collaboration in healthcare, particularly in times of crisis.

Valery Basheer introduced the concept of platform groups for rational functions over complex numbers, relating it to a rational function's ability to traverse invariant invariant submanifolds at a fixed point. He also proposed a conjecture stating that a rational function is equivalent to one with a non-trivial platform group only if it can be expressed as the composition of two bicritical rational functions. Our task is to resolve this conjecture by examining function iteration sequences and establishing a theoretical and practical method to calculate platform groups, ultimately proving the conjecture.

A novel empirical Bayes method for a high-dimensional linear model with model-specific error variances is developed and characterized.  For forecasting purposes, both least squares and minimum mean square error estimators are initially considered and compared.  Next, the research focuses on a novel estimator that achieves the minimum mean square error among all possible estimators, and which exhibits a non-asymptotic property, and converges to a finite limit as dimension increases.  This estimator can be efficiently computed, and its performance is evaluated through its statistical distance from the true parameter.  Theoretical and numerical examples illustrate the performance of various estimators, and demonstrate that the proposed empirical Bayes estimator outperforms other estimators, such as the least squares and minimum mean square error estimators, as the difference in predictive mean square error is significant and can be substantial.  The numerical findings also show that the finite-dimensional non-asymptotic property of the estimator is effective, and that it converges to a finite limit as the dimension increases.

In the Age of Industry 4.0, the machining sector is undergoing a significant transformation, with the integration of IoT technology and AI-driven automation driving more efficient production systems. A critical component of machining is the selection of appropriate equipment, which greatly influences operational costs and overall efficiency. To address the complexity of equipment selection, this research introduces a novel method combining the principles of Dependency Evaluation Theory and cost-benefit analysis. The objective is to identify optimal energy consumption options for machining hubs. The proposed approach utilizes a hierarchical structure to categorize and weigh criteria, with the relative importance of criteria determined through pairwise comparisons. A Bayesian evaluation model is employed to calculate the probability of criterion satisfaction, taking into account uncertainty, while a multi-objective genetic algorithm is used to identify and prioritize feasible solutions based on decision-maker preferences. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through a detailed analysis of equipment options for machining hubs in Turkey, with the results guiding decision-makers in selecting equipment that best aligns with their criteria.

The spectral dimension of a discrete-time random walk on a network is equal to two minus the largest eigenvalue in a certain linear function that describes the network's geometry. We prove this by establishing that this dimension is also determined by a fractal pattern of probabilities associated with the network, known as a regular conformal measure. Additionally, a probability distribution exists that describes how the conformal measure appears at different points on the network as a result of the random walk.

In the study of two-phase flow within a channel, we investigate how to effectively mix fluids with different viscosities by analyzing the impact of blending an immiscible pair of liquids. A mathematical model based on the Navier-Stokes and continuity equations is developed to simulate the two-phase flow and identify the conditions under which a specific type of flow pattern, known as the Taylor meniscus shape, occurs. This research demonstrates that by adjusting a parameter that determines the blend's viscosity, the likelihood of observing the Taylor shape can be increased. Our findings are validated through direct numerical simulations and supplemented by experiments to confirm the presence of this two-phase flow pattern.

This study seeks to characterize the uniqueness, complexity, and reliability of an online signature through comprehensive data collection and in-depth analysis. Specifically, individuals were asked to generate multiple signatures over a six-month period to capture natural variations in their writing patterns. This extensive dataset allows us to understand how signature characteristics evolve over time and how they change based on contextual factors. Our research employs statistical methods to assess the distinctiveness, intricacy, and stability of signatures, utilizing a large sample size and diverse subjects to ensure robust findings.

We investigate skew symmetric combinations of six copies of a particular spacetime theory, which is based on a description involving fields with higher-order characteristics. These constructions result in new theories that have space groups as their space symmetries, and we analyze their properties at the space level. Furthermore, we examine the potential for anomalies in their anomalies associated with space symmetries.

In one-dimensional systems with interacting charges, it is generally believed that only certain types of excitations, specifically spin and charge waves, can occur. However, we have discovered that when a stationary charge defect is introduced, higher-order connections between spin and charge can arise as a unique phenomenon. A charge defect effectively transforms the system into an elegant spin chain with an unusual pattern of magnetic properties. Notably, flipping the first magnet creates a ripple effect that extends over long distances, influencing every other magnet in the sequence in an alternating fashion. When combined with the presence of a charge carrier, this phenomenon results in spin and charge fluctuations that diminish at a much faster rate as the distance increases, specifically following a $1/r^4$ pattern.

In the past few years, the ABBNET project has provided new data on key nuclear reactions that occur in the B2V stellar process. By analyzing this data in the context of B2V stars with solar metallicity, we've found that the rate for the $^{14}$N($\alpha$,p)$^{17}$O reaction significantly slowed down at lower energies. This rate reduction led to lower amounts of nitrogen in the stars. However, the new rates still don't fully explain the observed high levels of nitrogen in certain B2V stars. To further investigate the matter, we've placed upper limits on the effective exothermic rates for two related nitrogen reactions. These bounds rely on the well-understood rate of a similar oxygen reaction and current precision measurements of related stable isotopes.

This paper provides a comprehensive, yet concise, overview of the obstacles and considerations inherent in code-mixing and code-switching phenomena, crucial for understanding these linguistic phenomena, especially those working on related projects, such as the NLP task for the NTCIR-18 Multilingual TREC evaluation.

Building upon pre-trained graph depiction and encoding has led to enhanced performance in various tasks, including node and graph classification. This success is largely attributed to using learned node and edge embeddings, which are pre-set and not learned in the context of a specific task. In this research, we take a different approach by treating graph depiction learning as a flexible task-specific problem, using task-related edge embeddings. We also develop a new task-oriented edge embedding, based on attention mechanisms, and demonstrate that it excels in two new benchmark tasks, particularly two-step gene-disease association prediction and gene enrichment analysis. Additionally, we find that incorporating pre-trained edge embeddings provides a beneficial boost, even outperforming performance achieved solely through task learning.

We've investigated the limitations that enhanced white dwarfs (WDs) can impose on two theoretical models: one where dark matter particles undergo inelastic transformations and another based on left-right symmetry. In the inelastic model, the mass difference between the dark matter particle and its antiparticle is set at 10 keV, and we've found the maximal permissible values for the mass of the dark matter particle to be approximately 35 and 30 GeV, depending on whether the particle is stable or undergoes inelastic transformation. In the L-R symmetric model, we've determined the maximal permissible values for the symmetry breaking scale to be around 10.5 TeV for a stable dark matter particle, and 10 and 8.5 TeV when the dark matter particle is massless or has a mass of 100 GeV, respectively. These outcomes imply that enhanced WDs can serve as a valuable tool in setting constraints on various theoretical models, and that future experiments using enhanced WDs could potentially provide more precise limitations.

Machine learning model training, utilizing real data, poses significant privacy risks to individual information. Graphs, as a type of data, combine attributes and entities to form meaningful connections. Current studies on graph-based privacy analysis and protection are limited due to the complex structure of graphs, which can include information leakage through entity relationships and attribute information. This paper presents a two-part approach for addressing real data privacy concerns. Firstly, a graph classifier is trained based on information labels, such as sensitivity or classification, to determine the content of each data item. This enables personalized privacy analysis, focusing on specific users or organizations. Secondly, a privacy optimization method is employed to balance privacy protection and information utility by removing or anonymizing classifier-identified data. This method is validated through two real-world datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in preserving content and structure, and is termed a Graph Privacy Consultant.

This paper examines the feasibility of secretly holding pure states, achieving absolute zero error in a quantum communication protocol where the sender has a limited number of copies and the receiver has access to unlimited copies. We first identify and discuss four potential models that facilitate this, and then demonstrate the existence of models where the task is doable. Notably, our findings show that combining a local, noiseless channel with a non-local noisy pathway can successfully hide a pure state in the concrete model we provided. We also explore the theoretical implications of using a hidden pathway with higher dimensionality, and the result indicates this is not feasible. Furthermore, the study reveals that noise can be effectively masked without requiring any action from the receiver in the local circuit, but the sender must be able to establish a link with the noisy source, and can only send a restricted number of copies.

Research on the fragmentation patterns of light-quark and gluon jets in proton-proton and proton-lead particle collisions is examined. These studies, conducted at 4.5 TeV and 2.76 TeV using the ATLAS detector at the LHC, employ tags from heavy-flavor decays to identify gluon-rich quark-$g$ systems. By comparing fragmentation patterns in $p+p$ and $p+Pb$ interactions, this research investigates the effect of color coherence on gluon fragmentation, utilizing a model that relates the $G/D$ ratio in protons to that in a hypothetical bag model of the lead nucleus. The study further identifies a small $p+Pb$ scale $Q$ and observes no notable $p+Pb$ dependence in the fragmentation patterns.

The highly versatile computational package, CP2K, has been developed within the chemical physics community for nearly two decades. With its ability to conduct simulations across ab initio quantum mechanics, quantum mechanics/solid theory, and molecular dynamics, the tool has seen applications expand beyond its origins into fields like quantum chemistry, biology, and materials science. This work details the evolution of CP2K's implementation on HPC systems, highlighting recent advancements in Linux portability, licensing adaptations, and developer contributions. Furthermore, the study examines the computational package's computational performance and development strategies, including the adaptation of CP2K to accommodate HPC systems with multiple CPU cores per node, vector instruction sets, and memory constraints. Lastly, the paper projects the potential of CP2K's computations to reach exascale levels, with a focus on upcoming HPC systems and the anticipated challenges and opportunities that may arise.

On June 14, 2019, the solar flare event GOX5.3 produced numerous Type III and II bursts, as well as significant emission in the 1-10 keV and 10-100 keV energy ranges. By analyzing data from the FOXSI3 board of the Focus Coil Solar Imager, researchers detected the onset of M-class solar flare emission at 1.5, 2.0, and 3.0 keV within 10 seconds. This corresponded to the brightest point source in the 12.8 arcsec field of view, exhibiting dynamic spatial changes. By comparing FOXSI data with RHESSI observations, researchers confirmed the presence of nonthermal electrons in the solar atmosphere, which produced the observed solar flare emission. Notably, the study detected the lowest intensity point source emission with FOXSI, matching the brightest emission at 1.5 and 2.0 keV with RHESSI at a significantly lower signal-to-noise ratio.

Predicting a graph neural network's performance on a specific dataset is a critical task in multiple fields. This problem, known as GNN extrapolation, encompasses two subtasks: GNN transfer (evaluating how well a graph neural model will perform on a different dataset from the same distribution) and social impact forecasting (determining which architectures to develop by assessing their potential real-world effects). Current research in social impact forecasting focuses on transferring pre-trained architectures, but we propose an innovative time expansion approach that allows for the efficient evaluation of a wide range of architectures, expanding the social impact of existing graph neural models. Our approach, evaluated on a real-world problem of predicting COVID-19's impact on U.S. states, demonstrates the effectiveness of time expansion in identifying useful but previously unconsidered architectures. Our method's potential applications extend to graph-based time series, natural images, and text.

The Euler-Arnold equations serve as a foundational model for understanding the integration problems associated with reducing Hamiltonian systems. Our research involves applying a specific geometric reduction technique to several equations derived from the Euler-Arnold framework, which represents a broad and comprehensive category. By doing so, we've successfully derived several reduction problems from different contexts, including one related to the space of flags in an 8-dimensional space under a specific symmetry, as well as issues connected to Hermitian connections within the space of Riemannian metrics and a system known as the Heavenly system. Furthermore, we've explored the relationship between these equations and the process of Hamiltonian reduction, particularly in the context of Hermitian connections.

This research focuses on developing efficient and reliable methods for pose estimation in point clouds. Initially, we adapt an existing algorithm, Completing the Square (CTSQ), which is used for complete regression, to regression by pose (RBP). Subsequently, we optimize the position regression step in CTSQ-RBP using an efficient technique based on Least Squares (LS). Furthermore, we extend our approach to handle inliers with varying reliability weights. Experimental results demonstrate a significant performance improvement, with substantial reductions in runtime and enhancements in accuracy.

The early universe's rapid expansion, known as inflation, has been the prevailing theory for over four decades. A key aspect of this inflationary model is the concept of "concealed sectors" - hidden dimensions or forces - which, according to recent research, may have influenced other visible forces and particles in a process called "reheating." A new study suggests that multiple forms of matter, such as dark and light particles, could have existed in thermal equilibrium, exchanging heat and particles in the early universe. This theory is further supported by new findings that indicate the phase transition between these distinct thermal states may have been gradual, rather than abrupt, and could have left behind unique patterns in the cosmic microwave background radiation. This radiation, a remnant of the early universe, has been extensively studied and provides crucial insights into the cosmic inflationary model.

The ATLAS experiment at the LHC, with 36.1 fb^-1 of data collected in 2015-2016, was used to study a rare process of electroweak same-sign W boson pair production. The study focused on events containing two same-sign W bosons, accompanied by two high-p_T jets and two leptons with the same charge. The observed number of events matched expectations from simulations, with the observed count falling slightly below the sum of standard model and background event predictions. The study set limits on the production rates of two top and semi-top quarks, with the former having exceeded a certain threshold and the latter having not exceeded a particular level at a specific confidence level in the 2017 publication.

We introduce a cross-camera profound colorization method that utilizes a diverse dataset of color and grayscale images captured from multiple cameras. The approach uses a dataset with a per-image correspondence system, allowing images to be directly correlated on a per-image basis rather than the traditional per-image correspondence system that relies on content matching and is thus blurry. The technique uses an ensemble of profound feature extraction networks that are trained independently from each camera, allowing them to operate without the need for alignment. The effectiveness of our proposed method was tested and it outperformed existing methods in experimental results.

Recent studies have shown that observational data can be better fitted if we deviate from the standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmological model, by adjusting its parameters to produce a more or less flat universe. To gain insight into the complexity of these findings, we conducted a Bayesian analysis using data from BAO, CMB, and $H_0$ to explore possible alternative spatial curvatures. Our analysis revealed that while the $\Lambda$CDM framework remains consistent with current observations, it doesn't fully account for the minimum distortion required by our analysis, suggesting a small positive curvature might be present.

The rapid growth of open-source projects on the GitHub platform is accompanied by a significant increase in maintenance requirements. A critical aspect of maintaining these projects is keeping their documentation up-to-date, yet researchers have found that the time spent on maintenance is often disproportionately lower compared to development time. To address this disparity, we introduce a novel concept of "meta-maintenance" for identifying open-source projects that require maintenance updates. Through a comprehensive analysis of 1,000 Java frameworks on GitHub, we found that a substantial portion of these projects suffer from documentation and source code desynchronization. To facilitate meta-maintenance, we developed an automated system that flags projects requiring maintenance attention. Our system's effectiveness is backed by the involvement of real-world contributors, namely the framework authors, who have validated our findings.

The 2019 10.6m Gemini North Telescope's time-domain spectroscopy of the eclipsing binary system BD~And revealed a unique two-star system with a 2.522222 day orbital period. High-resolution spectra revealed that both stars exhibit characteristics of F and F/G spectral types. The primary star displays significant rotational velocity and amplitude variations consistent with a gamma Doradus type oscillation. Analysis of secondary eclipses in multiple spectral bands allowed for precise determination of the system's geometric properties, resulting in a estimated surface gravity for both stars. These findings suggest that the stars in BD~And resemble gamma Doradus stars, particularly in their estimated radii and masses. Further research is necessary to confirm the exact nature of the oscillating mode in the primary star.

This study focuses on proving that the fractional Yamabe flow generates solutions that exist for all time, based on the conjectured gradient descent property of the $\sigma_k$-energy with $k=2$ or $3$. Based on this descent assumption, we can show that if the initial condition for the flow satisfies certain properties, the solution will exist indefinitely, and we will provide specific examples of when this assumption holds, including cases of star-shaped or radially symmetric manifolds with conformally related backgrounds.

Comprehensive aspect preferences are crucial in formulating purchase decisions, yet they remain underexplored in recommendation systems. Current methods, however, face the issue of incomplete or noisy user history that hinders their effectiveness. To overcome this limitation, researchers have proposed a novel approach called MSCL. This approach posits that users' deep preferences can be inferred by leveraging multiple data sources. By separating superficial and essential aspects of products, MSCL enables surface-level collaborative filtering to uncover hidden user preferences. These preferences are then employed in a sparse matrix factorization process that draws from various domains to offer more precise and comprehensive recommendations. This method not only outperforms the state-of-the-art in handling cold-start problems but also generates more explainable recommendations than a standard collaborative filtering system.

I establish the first-order deformation theory for orthogonal and symplectic vector bundle morphisms over arbitrary base spaces with unknown metrics, and demonstrate that the space of deformations is a closed subspace of the general vector bundle case. This result yields the deformation theory for perpendicular bundles. Furthermore, leveraging a fixed Hermitian connection and its associated unitary fibres, I obtain the deformation theory for symplectic morphisms. In the specific case of a trivial base with a fixed metric, my findings align with previously established theories.

Let S be a finite set of size n and consider all possible ways to split S into non-empty subsets based on an ordered k-ary tree structure, denoted as D(n,k). In this paper, we calculate the sum f(n,k) of components in all D(n,k) configurations, ensuring each node has less than k connected edges. Our result shows that (k+1) * (k!)^2 * f(n,k) is equal to k! * S(n,k) + sum of n choose r for r from 1 to n, multiplied by (k+1-2r) * D(r,k) * D(n-r, k). Furthermore, based on known results for S(n, k), we derive a recurrence relation to find the sequence d(n, k) associated with our study.

This work ensures non-asymptotic stability for $\ell_2$ estimation algorithms in contexts involving corrupted data samples, such as outcomes from heavy-tailed probability distributions or measurement errors with high variance. We develop a approach to transform any distribution with bounded support into a robust one, utilizing a modified measure of concentration originally proposed by Rudelson and Vershynski. Our approach relies on the concept of approximate mean-payoff games, providing a framework for analyzing estimation algorithms that do not specifically target tail concentrations, including methods like projected subgradient descent, FTVT, and least squares.

Recent data from the LHCb experiment have provided significant insights into the production and decay of the X(3872) particle, the LHC has made a discovery of the $h_{c}$ and established that a LHC-produced $B_{c}$ can decay into a $J/\psi$ and a $\delta^{\pm}$, in addition to this the LHC has provided an updated limit on the X(3872) particle's decay into a pair of photons. This note will discuss the LHC's latest findings and predictions for the LHC's potential to make further discoveries in the areas of quarkonium and exotic states.

Within disordered quantum systems, isolated rare events can occur, which typically have negligible impacts on typical physical properties. In contrast, the random singlet phase is an exceptional case where rare system configurations dominate the ground state. This phenomenon is extensively studied in one-dimensional disordered chains with short-range interactions, but in this work, we explore its boundaries with varying and disordered strength interactions. Our investigation focuses on how the nature of the RS phase changes as interactions go from being non-existent to strong and from being uniform to disuniform. We find that in one-type of non-linear interaction known as anisotropic interactions, the system exhibits coexisting phases, with the rare events of the RS phase and uncommon critical behaviors of the Kondo effect competing for dominance, their relative sizes depending on the degree of interaction anisotropy. In addition, we find that in systems with variable interaction strength, the disorder in coupling has an opposing effect on the disorder in interaction strength regarding the size of the rare event phase.

The set of reduced words for the reflection generators of a finite Weyl group correspondsingly maps to the set of reduced words for the simple Coxeter generators, with the map establishing a one-to-one connection. We establish a general binomial expression that calculates the number of reduced words in Weyl group order, using the parameters of a Coxeter matrix, and validate this formula through a generalization of Phylli's foundational theorem. Furthermore, we derived specific examples and generalizations for certain types of A_n, B_n, D_n groups as well as other Coxeter types, including F_4, F_3 (G_2), H_4, and H_3 (B_3).

In this research, we examined the scalar field description of non-linearly realized supersymmetry, focusing on two-dimensional space-time with $N=4$ symmetry. We discovered a previously reported two-soliton state and calculated its mass using a perturbation theory approach. The obtained result aligns with earlier findings from holographic dual theories. We further identified one-boson excitation modes associated with the two-soliton state. The found modes' quantum numbers correspond to those of the hypermultiplet dual theory. We also identified long-lived metastable states tied to two-soliton configurations. We derived the BPS equation governing these metastable states and demonstrated their connection to BPS operators within the hypermultiplet theory through perturbation theory. We established that these metastable states possess complex masses, a result consistent with previously published work.

This study is the first to introduce a novel, two-tiered, inverse reinforcement learning method that utilizes a hierarchical Bayesian approach. The upper level involves a cluster of agents that utilize predictive models to estimate a finite set of potentially regulated reward functions. As the agents' policies and corresponding observations are collected, a Bayesian inference algorithm determines each agent's influence on the reward function space. Meanwhile, at a lower granularity, specific tasks are tackled by reward function agents selected based on their relevance to the task at hand. These selected agents then collaborate to produce a reward function that can be utilized by a standard reinforcement learning algorithm to solve each task individually.

This research article builds upon the robustness of certain mappings related to M. A. Krasinkiewicz's concept of small loop transfer structures. These structures were initially introduced in relation to the primary fixed point set of continuous actions on a manifold, with a viewpoint from algebraic topology. The articles' novelty lies in extending the principles of these mappings to spaces with varying topological properties and introducing new variations, such as relative and locally equi-continuous transformations, with accompanying existence theorems for these variations.

In complex systems, designing an effective control strategy is a significant challenge. Applying traditional control theory to such complex systems is even more difficult. Recent breakthroughs in artificial intelligence, particularly through deep reinforcement learning, have made it possible to develop robust control policies for a wide range of applications. Nevertheless, certain problems persist when applying this technique, including difficulties in dealing with sparse and delayed rewards, ensuring action smoothness, and guaranteeing the safety of novel policies. This research proposes a comprehensive framework that integrates multiple strategies to address these issues. Building on existing research that uses autoencoders to discover and execute high-level actions, our framework incorporates techniques from traditional control theory to adapt these actions to the specific requirements of the problem. This framework draws on model predictive control to adapt the temporal characteristics of actions, utilizing optimal control theory to identify suitable high-level actions, and employing a technique that incorporates the intrinsic properties of the system through learned action representations. Additionally, our framework employs a technique that encodes and reuses past experiences to accelerate learning and enhance performance when sparse and delayed rewards are encountered. This research demonstrates the versatility of our framework, which can be safely and effectively applied to real-world problems, such as controlling a planar helicopter and navigating through a virtual environment.

Observations of dark holes spanning 12 orders of magnitude in mass have led to the discovery of supermassive dark holes at the centers of many galaxies. To understand the full mass distribution of dark holes and how they evolve over time, researchers are investigating the presence of intermediate-mass dark holes. In a follow-up study, the distribution of dark holes from 100 solar masses to over 100 billion solar masses is examined. By conducting a statistical analysis of the masses of dark holes, the researchers found that the seed masses for the dark holes we observe today likely range from 10 to 100 times the mass of the sun. They also determined that dark holes with masses between 10 and 1000 times the solar mass should be detectable by current telescopes, especially if they form early on and grow through accretion. Furthermore, the study suggests that the population of dark holes with masses between 10 and 1000 times the solar mass should peak around 100 million years after the universe began.

This work introduces a novel, modified neural network architecture, specifically designed for generalizing inelastic neutron scattering (INS) vibrational spectral data. By incorporating an intrinsic interpretability, the method enables identifying and focusing on the pivotal input features. In contrast to traditional supervised learning, this method relies on unsupervised learning techniques. We have successfully tested the method by applying it to a comprehensive dataset of organic and inorganic compounds. Our analysis involves visualizing the outcomes in both real and imaginary dimensions using principal component analysis. Additionally, we are capable of identifying distinct categories of phonon modes, such as gas-phase molecules, solids, and other specified features. Furthermore, the method facilitates identifying key spectral regions associated with specific modes and comparing the relative importance of different PCA components.

In the past thirty years, the number of researchers using online platforms to share their work has significantly increased, leading to a substantial number of articles being published before official publication. This has sparked debate over the long-term implications of such a vast amount of unpublished research. To better understand the growth and direction of the scientific community utilizing preprints, we analyzed a dataset comprising nearly 70,000 preprints published between 1991 and 2020 and published in nearly 1.5 million articles. Our findings reveal a notable disparity between the number of published preprints and those that have been published in journal articles. Notably, preprints published before 2001 nearly equaled the number of articles in the same time frame, whereas preprints published after 2001 have been outnumbered by nearly a factor of 20. This suggests that the characteristics of the community using preprints have undergone significant changes over time, with preprints becoming increasingly used as a means of sharing work that has been published in journal articles.

In recent years, there's been a notable upsurge in the number of digital journals due to their numerous advantages over traditional paper journals, encompassing ease of access, searchability, and editing. Despite these benefits, there's been a disparity between science and medicine fields in adopting digital publishing, with a significant number of papers still appearing on paper. A key factor contributing to this discrepancy is the limited functionality offered by current digital platforms, which often lack sophisticated tools for creating complex figures and equations. To address this gap, we've developed a system for generating high-quality digital figures using LaTeX, thereby facilitating the digital publishing process and paving the way for more seamless publication of digital content.

High-entropy alloys, characterized by their multi-component nature, exhibit exceptional mechanical, chemical, and physical properties. These advanced alloys, however, pose significant challenges in design and property prediction due to their complex composition. To overcome this obstacle, machine learning has been successfully applied, yielding notable results in identifying patterns, optimizing designs, and predicting unknown properties. This work delves into the current progress and applications of machine learning in high-entropy alloys, examines the inherent difficulties and potential solutions, and explores future research directions and collaborative opportunities.

We have calculated the decay rate of the $T_{cc}^+$ di-charmonium state into a final state consisting of a $D^{\ast+}D^-$ or $D^{\ast0}\bar{D}^0$ pair with an additional $\pi^-$ particle. Our phase-space limited estimation suggests a total branching ratio of approximately $1.2\times 10^{-4}$ for the $T_{cc}^+$ decay into a $D^{\ast+}D^-\pi^-$ configuration.

Machine learning has become a popular approach for modeling time series data, but it can be over-sensitive to noise and poorly justified when using black-box models. Researchers have developed a new type of graph neural network that uses differential equations to model time series data, but this previous work had limitations in dealing with uncertainty and modeling multiple factors simultaneously, as well as being susceptible to noise. Our work improves upon these limitations by creating a new chance-corrected graph neural network that can simultaneously model multiple systems, accounting for uncertainty in the data and using a graph to model the shared factors. The network uses a temporal point process to model the shared factors, allowing it to analyze both continuous and discrete data, and our numerical results show that our method outperforms existing techniques in terms of convergence speed, stability, and ability to detect changes in the data.

The nonlinearity of a vectorial Boolean function $F:\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m}$ is determined by its distance from the set of linear functions, and this distance is commonly expressed as $NL(F)=2^{n}-\max_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}}\operatorname{dist}(F,\ell)$, where $\mathcal{L}$ represents the set of all linear functions from $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m}$. The main goal of this paper is to establish a lower limit for the nonlinearity of a well-known type of vectorial Boolean functions called complete $q$-ary bent functions, specifically those with a valuation of $q$ and order 2. To achieve this, a new infinite collection of lower bounds is derived using the weights of specific binary bent functions, which in turn are lower bounded through application of a previously established result by Sturmfels. The result of this work is a novel, yet already substantial, lower bound on the nonlinearity of $q$-ary bent functions, and this finding has significant implications for the security assessment of cryptographic ciphers that utilize these types of functions.

In recent years, researchers have extensively studied the phase transition phenomenon in binary matrix problems, such as Plackett-Luce models, where sudden changes occur between solvable and unsolvable states. Building on this concept, we investigate the analogous behaviors in square binary matrices with a constant number of 1s per row and column. We demonstrate the existence of a critical point, n_c, which marks the phase transition. Below this threshold (n < n_c), a vast majority of matrices with a constant number of 1s per row and column are permutation-equivalent to at least one binary matrix with a strictly positive marginal constant. Furthermore, we show that for matrices with n > n_c, permutation-equivalence to such matrices is not possible. Additionally, we derive an analytical expression for n_c and verify it through both theoretical reasoning and computer simulations.

Introducing PDFs to interpret LHC data has become a crucial tool, yet their interpretation faces challenges in multiple-regions, multi-scale, and mixed-order scenarios. A new set of inconsistencies arises when different groups use varying formalism to interpret the same PDF set, leading to confusion in matching predictions with experimental data. To address these complexities, this paper proposes a comprehensive framework to facilitate LHC-based PDF adjustments by resolving adjustment kernels ambiguities through a clear, well-defined concept of a fluctuation field representing the difference between observed and expected event counts.

This document serves as the introductory to the ELKI library, an open-source, comprehensive data analysis package that can be utilized for anomaly detection, dimensionality reduction, clustering, and other data mining tasks. It is an easy-to-use, straightforward library, which is also user-friendly and can be incorporated into Java applications with minimal effort. This guide will provide an overview of the library, its features, and its recent release, version 0.7.5 from Heidelberg.

We've developed a new approach to create an optical frequency comb using a microresonator by merging a slow-varying amplitude envelope and a rapid carrier wave. In this study, we utilize the rapid parametric oscillations of a microresonator, triggered by a single laser, to synchronize and fine-tune a broad spectrum. We demonstrate these frequencies can be locked onto a single reference, effectively creating a new, unified frequency comb.

We establish a single, comprehensive class of discrete subgroups in groups that are acylindrically hyperbolic, characterized by stochastically, countably, and lloyally instability. This finding unifies and extends previous stochastic and lloyal subgroups discoveries, while also combining stability, instability, lloyalty, and countability aspects into one coherent category. The classification comprehensively covers all discrete subgroups, offering a full understanding of their structural properties within these groups.

This paper delves into the theoretical underpinnings of generalization in neural networks,
leveraging a probabilistic framework to quantify and analyze the geometric and stochastic properties of networks with binary weights.
By deriving an explicit description of the neural tangent kernel for such networks, we establish a direct link between the stochastic structure of the network and its kernel, which in turn influences the network's capacity and functional structure.
Through this understanding, we identify the stochastic entropy as a critical factor in determining generalization, which explains why quantization can improve network performance.
Our findings are substantiated by empirical evidence, which shows that our predictions align with observed trends in real-world applications.

In this research, we introduce extreme surfaces as extremal surfaces satisfying a local extremality condition at every point and argue that they also fulfill the global extremality requirement. We demonstrate that in specific 4D scenarios, such as Einstein duality models with linear charge assignments, global extreme surfaces coincide with conventional extreme surfaces, whereas local extremality may result in multiple solutions. We also identify an infinite family of charged asymptotically flat extreme surfaces associated with Reissner-Nordstrom black holes, as well as the first local solutions found outside the event horizon in the context of anti-de Sitter space.

The intersection multiplier is a measure used to quantify the complexity of a set of subgroups within a group, particularly when those subgroups are of prime order and intersect minimally among themselves. This concept is utilized to limit the number of possible labeled structures in a broad class of lattice models, a category that encompasses models like those for vertex and site coloring. Research has found that if a set of prime-order subgroups within a group G satisfies certain intersection constraints, then the number of such structures is limited to at most G to the power of n plus an exponential term with base 2 and base related to intersecting subsets in G. This is applicable when the group G has a fixed size of n. Furthermore, this research identifies specific resolvable lattice models that meet this bound, particularly those involving configurations like partitions of a set or flags within a projective space. These findings are also extended to applicable group varieties within the symmetric group S_n.

This research focuses on developing and analyzing stabilization techniques for certain nonsmooth and nonconvex iterative algorithms used in compressed sensing. We've established theoretical proofs that nonsmooth iterations can be successfully analyzed using the stochastic exterior fixed point theorem, whereas nonconvex iterations require the use of a stochastic generalized exterior hyperrandom field theorem. These findings are supported by concrete examples that demonstrate the application of our mathematical approaches.

In a recent paper by K. Glasse, a method is presented for combining images that calculates the combined image's intensity at each point by integrating the intensities of all input images corresponding to that point and beyond, weighted by distances. This approach is beneficial for efficiently processing point sources in the combined image without needing to input the original source's spatial distribution. However, determining the source size and shape from the combined image can be complicated due to the alteration of the point source flux distribution. The goal of this thesis is to investigate the effect of a source on a combined image and develop a way to obtain a combined image's point source PSF. A proposed solution involves using the input images' PSF at each point to calculate the combined image's PSF, which will then be compared with actual measurements of the PSF to validate the method.

We define new extensions of Gaussian free fields in the upper half-plane and a unit disk with boundary conditions, arising from chordal and radial multiple Schramm-Loewner-evolution processes. The field values at interior points are defined by specific probability distributions. We demonstrate that these probability distributions converge weakly to Gaussian distributions as points approach interior points, thereby establishing continuity at interior points. Furthermore, appropriate boundary conditions yield a continuous field on the upper half-plane and a unit disk, respectively. Our construction is linked with a local field whose distribution depends on the Loewner evolutions' chordal or radial nature and a parameter influenced by the driving orbits of the evolutions and the Beta distribution. We prove that this local field converges in law to the Gaussian free field with the specified boundary conditions as its scaling parameter tends to infinity.

In this study, pre-evaluations for Navier-Stokes equations' solutions with periodic initial conditions and specific classes of vector field starting points are obtained using the utmost norm. Moreover, the solution's existence and uniqueness are proven.

This proposal outlines a quantum-computing-based solution to a specific type of problem, known as the quadratic-form-constrained traditional validation problem (TVP), which arises in the solution of certain complex equations, including some forms of the Euler-Lagrange equations. We have developed an iterative algorithm to address this issue and integrated it into a quantum-computing model, which can be solved using a combination of the variational quantum eigensolver and eigenvalue problem techniques. Our approach leverages existing quantum algorithms, including those for generating Chebyshev polynomials, to converge on an optimal solution within a finite number of iterations. Furthermore, we explore the potential for accelerating this process by leveraging the phase estimation technique.

Achieving a comprehensive understanding of cellular processes relies heavily on accurate classification and segmentation of cells in images.
